summary: Peter and John go to the temple for afternoon prayer and meet a man unable to walk from birth. Peter has no money but commands him to walk in Jesus the Nazarene's name; the healed man enters the temple walking, leaping, and praising God. When a crowd gathers at Solomon's porch, Peter refuses credit, identifies Israel's God as the one who glorified Jesus, calls Jesus the Author of life, and summons his fellow Israelites to turn so that sins may be erased and promised restoration may come.
whyItMatters: The first narrated healing after Pentecost is both compassionate restoration and public sign. It brings a previously dependent man into temple praise and creates an occasion for witness, yet the apostles explicitly reject celebrity power. Peter's difficult accusation belongs to a familial appeal—‘brothers’ and ‘children of the prophets’—and ends not in ethnic rejection but an offer of blessing and turning.

context.author: The Luke–Acts narrator tracing witness in Jerusalem
context.audience: Readers learning how Jesus's name, Israel's Scriptures, healing, and repentance fit together
context.date: The narrated events belong to the earliest Jerusalem community
context.setting: The Beautiful Gate and Solomon's porch in the Jerusalem temple complex at the ninth-hour prayer time
context.literaryForm: Healing sign followed by an interpretive temple speech

outline.heading: A man unable to walk is healed in Jesus's name
Peter redirects the astonished crowd from the apostles to Israel's God
Peter calls Israel to turn within the prophets' promise

keyVerses.text: But Peter said, “I have no silver or gold, but what I have, that I give you. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, get up and walk!”
keyVerses.why: Apostolic authority is offered as restorative gift, not wealth or performance.

keyVerses.text: and killed the Prince of life, whom God raised from the dead, to which we are witnesses.
keyVerses.why: The paradox of killing life's author and God's resurrection of him anchors Peter's witness.

keyVerses.text: “Repent therefore, and turn again, that your sins may be blotted out, so that there may come times of refreshing from the presence of the Lord,
keyVerses.why: The accusation aims at forgiven return and renewed life.

questions.question: What does healing ‘in the name’ of Jesus mean?
questions.answer: In biblical usage a name can represent a person's authority and identity. Peter does not utter a magical password; he commands as Jesus's commissioned witness and immediately denies that personal power or piety caused the healing. The chapter attributes the restoration to Jesus's name and the faith associated with it.

questions.question: Why are Peter and John still going to the temple?
questions.answer: The earliest Jesus-followers remain Jewish worshipers who pray at the temple's appointed hour. Acts does not portray Pentecost as instant departure from Judaism; the sign and speech unfold inside Israel's worshiping life. Later conflicts concern claims about Jesus, authority, purity, and Gentile inclusion, not a simple replacement of ‘Judaism’ by ‘Christianity’ overnight.

questions.question: What changes for the healed man besides his legs?
questions.answer: He had been carried daily and positioned outside at a gate to request alms. After healing he stands, walks, and enters the temple with the apostles while praising God. Luke presents social, economic, bodily, and worshiping restoration together; the man is not merely an object lesson in someone else's sermon.

questions.question: Why does Peter call Jesus the ‘Prince’ or ‘Author’ of life?
questions.answer: The Greek archēgos can mean originator, leader, pioneer, or founder. The WEB's ‘Prince’ captures leadership, while ‘Author’ or ‘pioneer’ highlights Jesus as the one who opens life's path. The irony is deliberate: humans kill life's leader, but God raises him, overturning their verdict.

questions.question: How should readers handle Peter's accusation against Israelites?
questions.answer: Peter names denial and killing with painful directness, yet calls the crowd ‘brothers,’ acknowledges ignorance, says the prophets' suffering pattern has been fulfilled, and offers erased sins and covenant blessing. The Roman execution and Acts' many Jewish believers prevent collective ethnic blame. This is an internal Jewish prophetic appeal, not permission for Christians to condemn Jews as a people.

questions.question: What are ‘times of refreshing’ and ‘restoration of all things’?
questions.answer: Peter uses broad eschatological language for renewal from God's presence and the fulfillment spoken through the prophets. Interpretations differ over whether it emphasizes Israel's national restoration, creation's renewal, Christ's return, or their convergence. The text ties hope to repentance and to God's promised future without supplying a timetable.

questions.question: How does Peter use Moses's promised prophet?
questions.answer: He cites the Deuteronomic promise that God will raise a prophet like Moses and warns hearers to listen. Acts presents Jesus as the climactic prophet and servant within Israel's story. ‘Cut off’ is covenant warning, but Peter immediately identifies his hearers as heirs of the prophets and covenant rather than declaring them already abandoned.

questions.question: What does ‘servant’ contribute to Peter's portrait of Jesus?
questions.answer: The Greek pais can mean child or servant; in this speech it evokes the servant language of Isaiah and Israel's God glorifying his chosen agent. English traditions vary between ‘Son,’ ‘child,’ and ‘servant.’ The title joins Jesus to Israel's Scriptures rather than presenting him as an unrelated rival deity.

glossary.def: About 3 p.m., associated with afternoon temple prayer.

To change mind and direction, expressed here as turning back toward God.
